newsitem.title: THAILAND: Southeast Asian central bankers swap notes.
newsitem.headline: Southeast Asian central bankers swap notes.

text.p: Southeast Asian central bankers met on Thursday in Bangkok at a largely informal gathering to exchange views on their respective countries' economies.
"No fireworks. A friendly gathering of central bank colleages for informal talks about how we're doing," a central bank official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
He added there was no set agenda although he had learned earlier in the day that the officials would discuss asset price inflation.
Apart from the opening ceremony held on Thursday morning, the 32nd meeting of the 10-member Southeast Asian Central Bank Governors Conference (SEACEN) will be closed to the news media.
A delegate there as an observer told Reuters: "It's nice not having to talk to the press. We can relax and be ourselves."
The meeting kicked off with a welcome address by Thai central bank governor, Rerngchai Marakanond.
He noted economic restructuring had gradually transformed the Southeast Asian region from an agrarian society into an industrial powerhouse.
"Today, with vibrant growth and economic dynamism, the countries of our region attract the attention of the world community as top investment locations," he said.

"Central banks...have had to adapt their roles to evolve with this fast-changing world. I believe we are all thankful...there is this forum to turn to where we can discuss and exchange views on matters of mutual interest," he added.

Thailand's Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Amnuay Viravan told delegates at the opening ceremony that SEACEN economies continued to achieve satisfactory levels of growth, averaging close to seven percent in 1996.
"This is well above the world economic performance of 3.8 percent, according to the International Monetary Fund's estimates," he said.
SEACEN members are Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, South Korea, Taiwan, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Burma.
But Viravan noted inflation had been averaging around six percent over the last five years.

"Although this is considered high by industrial countries' standards, it is a phenomenon common of fast-growing economies with expanding domestic demand and operating at a high level of capacity utilisation,' he said.
He said reasons for the region's dynamism included high export growth, sound and consistent macro-economic policies and the pursuit of an open trade and investment regime.

"These factors, together with strong economic fundamentals and vast investment opportunities, serve to attract more private capital inflows, which, in turn, help to fuel growth and strengthen the reserve position," he added.
The meeting is due to end on Friday.
